methodological_rigor.justification: The study uses appropriate murine knockout, in vitro Th polarization, adoptive-transfer colitis, RNA-seq, Seahorse, comet, co-immunoprecipitation, docking, and rescue experiments to test the XPC-Th17 mechanism. It reports biological replicate numbers for some core assays, RNA-seq used five independent biological replicates, and the statistics section states normality testing, t-tests, ANOVA with Tukey post hoc testing, and effect-size estimates where appropriate. Important limitations are explicitly present: no sample-size predetermination, no randomization or blinding, many flow and imaging assays use small n values or technical replicates, and some immunoblots are described as representative single experiments.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The dominant design is preclinical and mechanistic, using murine XPC-deficient cells, Rag1-/- colitis transfer, in vitro T-cell polarization, and reanalysis of public Crohn's disease single-cell data, so the Oxford level is 5. The work has plausible translational relevance because it links DNA repair, oxidative stress, and Th17 differentiation, with implications for inflammatory disease and cancer susceptibility in xeroderma pigmentosum. The endpoints are mechanistic immune phenotypes and murine inflammation rather than patient outcomes or therapeutic efficacy in oncology patients.

reporting_quality.justification: ARRIVE is the closest standard because the manuscript includes animal experiments along with cell and omics work. Ethics approvals, mouse strains, ages, weights, adoptive-transfer procedures, assay protocols, and statistical tests are described, and a Nature Portfolio reporting summary is referenced. Reporting gaps include no predetermination of sample size and no randomization or blinding, both stated in the statistical analysis section. RNA-seq data are deposited at SRA under PRJNA1160718 and public Crohn's disease scRNA-seq data are cited, but analysis code and full protocols are not provided in the normalized text.

novelty_literature.justification: The manuscript meaningfully extends prior work on XPC, oxidative DNA damage repair, and Th17 biology by proposing a BATF-XPC axis that coordinates redox control and OGG1-linked base excision repair during Th17 differentiation. The novelty is mechanistic rather than first-in-class, since prior studies already established XPC roles in oxidative damage, XPC-OGG1 interaction, and ROS effects on Th17 cells. The new contribution is the integration of these mechanisms in Th17 differentiation and an inflammatory transfer model.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract is clear and accurately frames the central mechanistic claim, and the results generally progress from phenotype to mechanism to rescue. Methods are detailed enough for many assays, including antibodies, culture conditions, RNA-seq workflow, docking tools, and statistical tests. Presentation is weakened by some awkward phrasing, repeated methods and ethics content, occasional typographic issues, and figure captions that mix biological and technical replicate language in ways that can be hard to interpret.

key_strengths: Uses multiple complementary assays to connect XPC deficiency with impaired Th17 differentiation, oxidative DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and OGG1 activity.
Includes an in vivo Rag1-/- adoptive-transfer colitis model showing functional consequences of XPC-deficient CD4+ T cells.
Provides RNA-seq data deposition and detailed experimental protocols for many cell and molecular assays.
key_concerns: No sample-size predetermination, randomization, or blinding is reported despite animal and imaging-based endpoints.
Several key assays rely on small n values or technical replicates, and some Western blot quantifications derive from representative single experiments.
The translational claims for cancer susceptibility and human Th17 disease remain indirect and are not tested in patient cohorts.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a competent mechanistic preclinical study with a coherent biological model but moderate rigor and reporting limitations. It is plausible for a tier 3 venue after major revisions addressing experimental design transparency and replicate structure.
